subtopic_detail: New dyspepsia in an older man taking an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation who has added an antidepressant and a self bought analgesic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 72 year old man in a shared care clinic six weeks after starting sertraline for a depressive episode. His mood has improved and he is sleeping better.

He mentions that he has been buying ibuprofen from the supermarket twice daily for the past three weeks for knee pain, and that for the last week he has had burning discomfort in his upper abdomen after meals. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He has had no black stools, no vomiting of blood and no dizziness, and his knee pain is manageable when he rests.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness with no guarding, no abdominal mass, rectal examination declined, conjunctivae not pale, euthymic affect with no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 139 g/L (130 to 180), platelets 218 x10^9/L (150 to 400), creatinine 94 micromol/L (60 to 110) with an estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60 mL/min/1.73m2, ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30 to 300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the apixaban and substitute aspirin for stroke prevention, continuing both the sertraline and the analgesic for his knee
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to a direct oral anticoagulant for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and still carries gastrointestinal bleeding risk, so this trades a large stroke risk for a small change in bleeding risk. The anticoagulant is the one agent of the three with a clear mortality benefit that should be preserved. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines

options.text: Cease the ibuprofen, review his knee pain with a non ulcerogenic alternative and reassess his upper abdominal symptoms shortly afterwards
options.rationale: The non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is the newest, most dispensable and most ulcerogenic element of a triple combination in which each agent independently raises gastrointestinal bleeding risk, and its removal addresses both the symptom and the risk. Paracetamol, topical therapy and exercise based management can cover the knee without the same hazard. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the sertraline and substitute a different antidepressant class, continuing the anticoagulant and the analgesic as he is now taking them
options.rationale: Stopping an antidepressant that is working risks relapse of a depressive episode in an older man, and the serotonin reuptake inhibitor contributes far less to the bleeding risk than the non steroidal drug does. Substituting the antidepressant would become reasonable if bleeding recurred after the analgesic had already been removed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add a proton pump inhibitor and continue all three medications, reviewing his upper abdominal symptoms in the clinic in eight weeks
options.rationale: Gastroprotection reduces but does not abolish the bleeding risk of the combination, and it does nothing about the antiplatelet effect of the non steroidal drug on the whole gastrointestinal tract below the stomach. Adding a proton pump inhibitor is the right move when the non steroidal drug genuinely cannot be stopped. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Peptic ulcer disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Peptic ulcer disease

options.text: Switch the apixaban to warfarin with regular monitoring of the international normalised ratio and continue the other two medications unchanged
options.rationale: Warfarin carries a higher rate of intracranial and overall major bleeding than apixaban in atrial fibrillation, so the switch increases rather than reduces harm. Warfarin remains preferred for mechanical heart valves and severe renal impairment, not for avoiding gastrointestinal bleeding. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors deplete platelet serotonin, which is required for normal platelet aggregation, and so raise the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding by roughly one and a half times on their own. That modest effect becomes clinically important when it is combined with other agents acting on the same endpoint, and the combination of an anticoagulant, a non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and a serotonergic antidepressant is one of the highest risk prescribing triads in general practice. The clinical skill is deciding which agent to remove: the anticoagulant carries a mortality benefit that should almost never be sacrificed, the antidepressant is treating an active illness and is working, and the non steroidal drug is both the largest contributor to ulcer risk and the one with a ready alternative. Over the counter purchase is a particular trap because patients do not consider supermarket analgesics to be medication and do not mention them unless asked directly. New dyspepsia in this setting is a warning shot that should prompt action before an overt bleed occurs.
key_points: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors impair platelet aggregation by depleting platelet serotonin.
Anticoagulant plus non steroidal drug plus serotonergic antidepressant is a high risk triad.
Ask specifically about over the counter analgesics, which patients rarely volunteer.
Remove the non steroidal drug first, since it carries the greatest ulcer risk and has alternatives.
Gastroprotection is for when the non steroidal drug genuinely cannot be stopped.
explanation.pearls: If a non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is unavoidable in a patient on an anticoagulant, a proton pump inhibitor halves the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding but offers no protection against small bowel or colonic bleeding, which accounts for a substantial share of the excess events in this combination.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Peptic ulcer disease

subtopic_detail: Choosing an antipsychotic for a man on high dose opioid substitution whose corrected QT interval is already 480 milliseconds
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 45 year old man with schizophrenia who has been stable off antipsychotic medication for two years but has relapsed over the past month with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He is distressed and asking for help.

He has been on methadone 120 mg daily for eight years through a community clinic and has been abstinent from other drugs. He has no cardiac symptoms and no family history of sudden death. His previous good response was to an oral second generation antipsychotic that he stopped himself when he felt well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Guarded and preoccupied with persecutory beliefs, no thought disorder, no extrapyramidal signs, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 480 milliseconds, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the methadone dose by half over the next week so that the corrected QT interval falls before any antipsychotic is commenced
options.rationale: Halving a long standing methadone dose precipitates withdrawal and greatly raises the risk of relapse to illicit opioid use and overdose, and it delays treatment of an acute psychotic episode. Gradual dose reduction in discussion with the opioid treatment prescriber is considered when the interval exceeds 500 milliseconds or after an arrhythmic event. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol for rapid control of his psychotic symptoms and repeat the electrocardiogram after the first few doses
options.rationale: Haloperidol given parenterally carries the highest risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes of the commonly used antipsychotics, which is precisely the wrong property here. Parenteral haloperidol is reserved for acute behavioural emergencies in patients without a prolonged interval and with cardiac monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Correct his potassium and magnesium, then commence aripiprazole and repeat the electrocardiogram once he is established on treatment
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are modifiable contributors to QT prolongation and should be corrected first, and aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of the available antipsychotics, making it the rational choice alongside high dose methadone. Repeating the electrocardiogram after establishing the dose confirms that the interval has not worsened. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence high dose oral quetiapine titrated rapidly over one week and monitor the electrocardiogram weekly for the first month of treatment
options.rationale: Quetiapine prolongs the QT interval in a dose dependent way and rapid titration to a high dose in a man already at 480 milliseconds adds avoidable risk. Quetiapine is a reasonable choice in patients without baseline QT prolongation or concurrent QT prolonging drugs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold antipsychotic treatment entirely and offer psychological therapy alone until his corrected QT interval falls below 450 milliseconds
options.rationale: Leaving an acute psychotic relapse untreated carries substantial risk to the patient and prolongs the duration of untreated psychosis, which worsens long term outcome. Psychological therapy is a valuable adjunct but is not a substitute for antipsychotic treatment in an acute relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

explanation.summary: Methadone blocks the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current in a dose dependent way and is the main reason that people on opioid substitution therapy carry an elevated baseline corrected QT interval, with the risk rising appreciably above doses of around 100 mg daily. When an antipsychotic is needed in this population the task is to add as little further repolarisation delay as possible while treating the psychosis effectively. Aripiprazole, and to a lesser extent olanzapine and lurasidone, have minimal effect on the QT interval, whereas haloperidol given parenterally, high dose quetiapine, ziprasidone and pimozide are the agents to avoid. Electrolyte disturbance is the most easily reversible contributor and should always be corrected, since hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia compound any drug effect. Thresholds worth knowing are a corrected interval above 500 milliseconds or an increase of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline, either of which demands reassessment of every contributing drug.
key_points: Methadone prolongs the QT interval in a dose dependent manner, particularly above 100 mg daily.
Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia before attributing the interval to drugs alone.
Aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of available antipsychotics.
Parenteral haloperidol, high dose quetiapine and ziprasidone should be avoided in this setting.
An interval above 500 milliseconds or a rise of more than 60 milliseconds demands drug review.
explanation.pearls: Check for a cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitor whenever the corrected QT interval rises unexpectedly in a patient on methadone, because agents such as fluconazole, clarithromycin and some antiretrovirals raise methadone concentrations substantially and the interval falls again when the interacting drug is stopped.

subtopic_detail: Seeing people in the house three weeks after an increase in a dopamine agonist in a man with established Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 76 year old man with a nine year history of Parkinson disease whose wife reports that he has been seeing people standing in the hallway in the evenings. He describes them clearly, knows they are not really there when she points it out, and is not frightened by them.

His motor symptoms had worsened over the summer and his neurologist increased the dose of his dopamine agonist three weeks ago. There has been no fever, no urinary symptoms, no fall and no change in his other medications. His wife says he is his usual self during the day with no drowsiness and no confusion about where he is.

data_table.Examination: Orientated to time place and person with attention sustained through serial sevens, Montreal cognitive assessment 25 out of 30 and unchanged from a score recorded eight months ago, bradykinesia with a resting tremor and mild rigidity, no myoclonus, no fever, chest clear, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110), midstream urine microscopy showing no organisms and no white cells, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Commence risperidone at a low dose and titrate slowly according to the frequency of the hallucinations over the following month
options.rationale: Risperidone has high dopamine D2 receptor affinity and reliably worsens parkinsonian motor symptoms, sometimes severely and irreversibly in this population. It has no place in the treatment of hallucinations in Parkinson disease at any dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce and then withdraw the dopamine agonist in discussion with his neurologist and review his hallucinations after the dose change
options.rationale: Hallucinations that begin within weeks of increasing a dopaminergic drug, in a patient with preserved insight, stable cognition and no evidence of infection or metabolic disturbance, are drug induced until proven otherwise, and dopamine agonists are the most hallucinogenic of the Parkinson medications. Reducing the offending drug before adding another is the correct order of operations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence olanzapine at a low dose in the evening and review both his motor function and his hallucinations in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Olanzapine worsens motor function in Parkinson disease more than quetiapine or clozapine and is not recommended in this setting. If an antipsychotic is eventually required after dopaminergic reduction, quetiapine or clozapine are the agents with the least motor penalty. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence quetiapine at a low dose tonight and keep the dopamine agonist at its current dose so that his motor control is not compromised
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the usual antipsychotic choice in Parkinson disease, but adding it while leaving the precipitating drug untouched treats the symptom and accepts the sedation and falls risk unnecessarily. It becomes appropriate when hallucinations persist or distress the patient after dopaminergic reduction has been attempted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor and arrange formal neuropsychological assessment to characterise the cognitive profile more fully
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors help hallucinations in Parkinson disease dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies, but his cognitive score is unchanged over eight months and there is no fluctuating attention, so dementia does not explain this. That treatment becomes appropriate once a dementia has been established and the drug review has been completed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Visual hallucinations are common in Parkinson disease and have three broad drivers: dopaminergic medication, an emerging dementia, and an acute precipitant such as infection, metabolic disturbance or a new sedating drug. Sorting between them determines the treatment entirely, so the sequence is to exclude a delirium, review the cognitive trajectory and then scrutinise the medication timeline. Dopamine agonists carry a higher risk of hallucinations and of impulse control disorders than levodopa does, which is why they are the first drug to be reduced when psychotic symptoms emerge, followed if necessary by anticholinergics, amantadine and monoamine oxidase B inhibitors, with levodopa reduced last because motor function depends on it. Only when dopaminergic reduction is insufficient or motor deterioration makes it impossible is an antipsychotic added, and then quetiapine or clozapine are used because all other agents worsen parkinsonism. Preserved insight, as in this man, marks an earlier and more benign stage, whereas the loss of insight signals progression and a worse prognosis.
key_points: Exclude delirium and review the cognitive trajectory before attributing hallucinations to the disease.
Hallucinations starting within weeks of a dopaminergic increase are drug induced until proven otherwise.
Dopamine agonists are more hallucinogenic than levodopa and are reduced first.
Levodopa is reduced last because motor function depends on it.
Only quetiapine and clozapine are acceptable antipsychotics in Parkinson disease.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about new gambling, shopping, eating or sexual behaviour at every review of a patient on a dopamine agonist, because impulse control disorders affect around one in six of those treated, are almost never volunteered spontaneously and resolve when the agonist is withdrawn.

subtopic_detail: Persecutory beliefs emerging on week two of sight saving high dose steroid treatment that cannot be withdrawn
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 71 year old woman on the medical ward. She was started on prednisolone 60 mg daily twelve days ago for biopsy proven giant cell arteritis after presenting with jaw claudication and transient visual loss.

Over the past four days she has become convinced that the nursing staff are recording her conversations and plotting to move her to a locked facility, and last night she tried to leave the ward at 2 am. Her treating physician tells you that the steroid dose cannot be reduced meaningfully for several more weeks without risking her sight, and that she has no prior psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Fully orientated with attention sustained through months of the year backwards, no fluctuation in conscious state documented over three nursing shifts, fixed persecutory beliefs held with full conviction, no visual hallucinations, no tremor or asterixis, no neck stiffness, temporal arteries non tender on palpation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (less than 5) having fallen from 96 mg/L on admission, sodium 137 mmol/L (135 to 145), calcium corrected 2.38 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), glucose 9.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain reported as showing age related atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the prednisolone immediately, since the psychiatric adverse effect outweighs the benefit, and manage her arteritis with an anti-inflammatory
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of high dose corticosteroid after twelve days risks both irreversible visual loss from uncontrolled arteritis and adrenal insufficiency, and no anti-inflammatory substitutes for corticosteroid in giant cell arteritis. The steroid is sight saving and must continue while the psychiatric complication is treated alongside it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

options.text: Treat the presentation as a hyperactive delirium with orientation measures and environmental modification, and avoid any psychotropic medication
options.rationale: Delirium is the key differential on a medical ward, but her attention is intact, her conscious state has not fluctuated across three shifts and her inflammatory markers and imaging are unremarkable, which is the combination that excludes it. Delirium management would be correct if attention were impaired and the picture waxed and waned. (Source: RANZCP: Delirium in older people)

options.text: Commence a low dose atypical antipsychotic, continue the steroid at the dose her sight requires, and plan to withdraw the antipsychotic as it is reduced
options.rationale: Corticosteroid induced psychosis responds well to low dose antipsychotic treatment, so where the steroid cannot be reduced the correct course is to continue it at the dose the underlying disease demands and treat the psychosis concurrently. The antipsychotic is then tapered as the steroid dose falls, rather than continued indefinitely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence lithium at a therapeutic dose with serum level monitoring as prophylaxis against further steroid related psychiatric disturbance
options.rationale: Lithium has been used prophylactically in patients with recurrent steroid induced mood disturbance requiring repeated courses, but it acts too slowly for an acute psychosis and carries significant toxicity risk in an older woman. It is a consideration for planned future courses, not for the episode in front of you. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange transfer to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit for management of a first episode psychosis in later life with ongoing medical liaison
options.rationale: Transferring a woman who needs daily titration of sight saving immunosuppression to a unit without that medical capability endangers her vision and fragments her care. Transfer would be appropriate if the psychiatric risk could not be managed on the medical ward once her arteritis was stable. (Source: RANZCP: Delirium in older people)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disturbance is strongly dose dependent, affecting a few per cent of patients below 40 mg of prednisolone daily and close to a fifth of those above 80 mg, and it typically emerges within the first two weeks of treatment. Mood elevation and irritability are the commonest presentations, but frank psychosis with persecutory delusions occurs and is more likely at higher doses and in older patients. The essential differential on a medical ward is delirium, and the discriminators are attention and fluctuation: a steroid psychosis has a clear sensorium and a stable conscious state, whereas delirium impairs attention and waxes and wanes across the day. Management is guided by whether the steroid can be reduced, and where it cannot, as in sight threatening giant cell arteritis, the psychosis is treated concurrently with a low dose antipsychotic that is withdrawn as the steroid is tapered. Prior psychiatric history is a surprisingly weak predictor, so its absence offers no reassurance.
key_points: Risk rises steeply with dose, approaching one in five above 80 mg of prednisolone daily.
Onset is usually within the first two weeks of treatment.
Intact attention with a stable conscious state distinguishes steroid psychosis from delirium.
Where the steroid is sight saving it continues and the psychosis is treated concurrently.
Taper the antipsychotic as the steroid dose falls rather than continuing it indefinitely.
explanation.pearls: An absent psychiatric history gives no protection against steroid induced psychosis, and conversely a past episode does not reliably predict recurrence on a later course, so the practical safeguard is to warn every patient starting more than 40 mg of prednisolone daily and to ask a relative to report behavioural change in the first fortnight.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

subtopic_detail: Registrar colleague smelling of alcohol while rostered to the ward with a slurred handover witnessed by two staff
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an evening shift. During handover a fellow registrar rostered to the ward until midnight smells strongly of alcohol, slurs several words and twice loses his place in the patient list. The nurse in charge quietly tells you she noticed the same thing last Friday.

When you speak to him privately he becomes upset, says he had two drinks at lunch because his marriage has broken down, insists he is fine to work and begs you not to say anything. He is due to review two involuntary patients tonight and holds the ward pager.

data_table.Examination: Slurred speech with an unsteady gait on walking to the office, alcohol on the breath, tearful and reactive affect, no suicidal ideation elicited on direct questioning, orientated with no gross cognitive impairment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Accept his reassurance, offer to review any complex patients with him tonight and encourage him to seek help from his general practitioner
options.rationale: Supervising a colleague who is intoxicated does not make the care safe, and his self assessment of fitness is itself impaired by the alcohol. Informal support is appropriate for a colleague who is struggling but sober and safe to practise. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Advise him to complete this shift and then take personal leave, and agree that nothing needs to be reported if he starts treatment this week
options.rationale: Allowing him to complete a shift while intoxicated leaves patients exposed for the very hours in which the risk is highest, and a promise of confidentiality is one you cannot keep once the mandatory threshold is met. Supporting a colleague into treatment is a parallel obligation, not an alternative to protecting patients. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Ask the nurse in charge to observe him for the remainder of the shift and document any further concerns for discussion at the next team meeting
options.rationale: Delegating observation to a nurse places the responsibility on a colleague with less authority to act and leaves the patients at risk during the observation period. Documentation and escalation at a later meeting is appropriate for a pattern of performance concerns, not for present intoxication. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Remove him from clinical duties now by escalating to the on call consultant, arrange his safe transport home and make a mandatory notification
options.rationale: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is one of the four categories of notifiable conduct under the national law, and the obligation arises from a reasonable belief rather than from proof, so the notification is mandatory and not discretionary. Removing him from duty and arranging safe transport protects both the patients and the colleague. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Arrange an immediate breath alcohol test and take no further action if the reading falls below the legal limit for driving a motor vehicle
options.rationale: There is no legal blood alcohol threshold for clinical practice and the driving limit has no bearing on fitness to make clinical decisions. Objective testing may form part of a health programme later, but it does not replace the judgement that a doctor is impaired now. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

explanation.summary: Under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, registered practitioners must make a mandatory notification when they form a reasonable belief that another practitioner has engaged in notifiable conduct, which comprises practising while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, engaging in sexual misconduct in connection with practice, placing the public at risk of substantial harm because of an impairment, or placing the public at risk because of a significant departure from accepted professional standards. The threshold is a reasonable belief rather than proof, and the obligation cannot be discharged by a promise of confidentiality or by agreeing to supervise the colleague. Immediate patient safety comes first, which means removing the practitioner from clinical duties through the on call consultant or hospital executive and arranging safe transport home rather than allowing them to drive. Compassion and regulation are not in conflict here, since notification opens access to structured health programmes with monitored return to work pathways, and outcomes for doctors with substance use disorders who enter such programmes are good. Western Australia has different arrangements for treating practitioners, and practitioners seeking their own treatment are protected in most jurisdictions to encourage help seeking.
key_points: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is notifiable conduct under the national law.
The threshold is a reasonable belief, not proof, and the obligation is mandatory.
Immediate action is removal from clinical duties and arranging safe transport home.
A promise of confidentiality cannot override a mandatory notification obligation.
Notification opens access to health programmes with good return to work outcomes.
explanation.pearls: Treating practitioners in most Australian jurisdictions are exempt from mandatory notification when a doctor patient seeks treatment for an impairment and is not currently placing the public at substantial risk, an exemption designed specifically so that unwell doctors present for care rather than concealing illness.

sources.label: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice code of conduct

subtopic_detail: Episodes labelled as panic attacks that bring pallor and severe hypertension and that worsened after an antidepressant was started
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 42 year old woman referred with treatment resistant panic disorder. For eighteen months she has had episodes of pounding heartbeat, throbbing headache and drenching sweats lasting about twenty minutes, and she has had two adequate trials of cognitive behavioural therapy with no benefit.

Her husband says she goes chalk white during the attacks rather than flushed. The episodes come without warning, including from sleep, and she can identify no situational trigger and avoids nothing. Her general practitioner started venlafaxine eight weeks ago and the attacks have since become more frequent and more severe. She has lost 6 kg over the year without dieting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Anxious but fully orientated, pale with cool peripheries, no tremor of the outstretched hands beyond a fine physiological tremor, no goitre, no lid lag, no exophthalmos, fundoscopy showing arteriovenous nipping, body mass index 21 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, fasting glucose 6.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45 to 90), urine drug screen negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the venlafaxine dose and add a short course of a benzodiazepine while the higher antidepressant dose takes effect over coming weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors block noradrenaline reuptake and can provoke hypertensive crises where catecholamine secreting tumours are present, which is the most plausible explanation for her symptoms worsening after it was started. Dose escalation would be the correct response to a partial response in genuine panic disorder with a normal blood pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure plasma free metanephrines under standardised conditions, withhold the venlafaxine and refer her urgently to an endocrinology service
options.rationale: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with pallor rather than flushing, unprovoked nocturnal attacks, sustained hypertension with end organ change, weight loss and deterioration after a noradrenergic drug together point to a catecholamine secreting tumour rather than panic disorder. Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive screening test and the interfering drug should be withdrawn. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence a non selective beta blocker to control both the cardiovascular symptoms and the somatic anxiety that accompanies each episode
options.rationale: Unopposed beta blockade in the presence of a catecholamine secreting tumour removes beta mediated vasodilation and leaves alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Beta blockade is added only after adequate alpha blockade has been established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer her for a third course of psychological therapy with a different therapist and add an antihypertensive for the raised blood pressure
options.rationale: Treating the blood pressure as an incidental comorbidity and the episodes as psychological misses the single diagnosis that unifies both, and two failed adequate therapy trials should prompt review of the diagnosis rather than a third attempt. A further therapy course would be reasonable if the somatic workup were genuinely unremarkable. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen as the initial investigation to look for an adrenal mass before any biochemical testing is undertaken
options.rationale: Imaging before biochemistry inverts the diagnostic sequence and risks finding an incidentaloma that is present in several per cent of adults and is unrelated to her symptoms. Imaging follows biochemical confirmation and is then directed at localising a tumour already proven to be secreting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma are rare but are disproportionately likely to be referred to psychiatry, because the paroxysmal adrenergic symptoms they produce are almost indistinguishable from panic attacks and patients are frequently labelled with an anxiety disorder for years. Several features separate them: attacks in panic disorder are typically situationally cued or arise in a context of anticipatory anxiety and avoidance, whereas catecholamine driven attacks are truly unprovoked, often wake the patient from sleep, and produce pallor rather than flushing. Sustained hypertension between attacks with evidence of end organ damage, unexplained weight loss and impaired glucose tolerance from catecholamine mediated insulin suppression all point away from a primary anxiety disorder. Drugs that block noradrenaline reuptake, including serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors and tricyclics, can precipitate crises and also interfere with the assay, so they are withdrawn before testing where it is safe to do so. Plasma free metanephrines drawn supine after rest are the most sensitive screen, and imaging follows biochemical confirmation, with alpha blockade preceding any beta blockade and preceding surgery.
key_points: Truly unprovoked attacks that wake the patient from sleep argue against panic disorder.
Pallor during attacks rather than flushing is an important discriminating sign.
Sustained hypertension with end organ change, weight loss and hyperglycaemia support a secreting tumour.
Noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors can precipitate crises and interfere with the assay.
Biochemistry precedes imaging, and alpha blockade always precedes beta blockade.
explanation.pearls: Around 40 per cent of phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas carry a germline mutation, in genes including succinate dehydrogenase subunits, VHL, RET and NF1, so every confirmed case is referred for genetic counselling regardless of age or family history.
